Subject: Atlas Retail — SSE heartbeat / initial-emission latency & chunk pacing (post-demo recap)

Hi Samira / Tom — thanks again for the call earlier. Quick written recap + proposed next steps so we have a single artifact.

Summary of what we heard (verification):
- Peak search/query concurrency: ~50 concurrent users spawning model requests (bursts up to 120 for Flash Sales).
- Target steady throughput: 150 req/s during campaigns, spiking to ~350 req/s for 30–60s microbursts.
- Desired latency SLOs: initial emission (first token emitted to client) in <= 120 ms p95 for typical short prompts (~25 tokens). End-to-end generation latency target per request: <= 700 ms p95.
- Streaming preference: prefer SSE for browser clients (simpler integration); may use WebSocket for mobile SDKs where connection stickiness is higher. Heartbeat/keepalive expectations: 20s max so client knows connection is healthy.
- Chunk cadence: client wants small frequent chunks for UI progressive render (roughly 150–300 ms between chunks; prefer 2–4 tokens per chunk average).

Open items we promised to investigate / confirm:
1) Whether 120 ms p95 initial emission is realistic across our hosted profile given their prompt mix and expected concurrency (we'll run a focused probe).
2) Backpressure behavior when the model emits larger completions (how we shape chunks and throttle).
3) Recommended SSE heartbeat cadence vs. client keepalive and how fallbacks to poll/push work if connections drop.
4) Example network trace and an SLO proposal for their pilot (attached).

Immediate next steps from Redwood:
- Run a simulated probe matching Atlas traffic profile (concurrency + burst patterns) and share a measured p50/p95/p99 for first emission and full-response latencies. Target ETA: 48–72 hours.
- Rishi will draft a short SLO proposal with chunk cadence options and fallback modes (SSE vs WebSocket).
- Share small attachment: sample KV-prefix trace to show how prefix caching could reduce emit latency for repeated prompts.

Can you confirm the burst figures above and whether 120 ms p95 target is a hard requirement for the pilot, or negotiable for an MVP? Also confirm whether the web client can accept 200 ms heartbeat instead of 20s — we want to align on realistic keepalive behavior.

Thanks — I’ll kick off the probe as soon as you confirm.

Best,

Thanks, Irene — this is very helpful. Quick answers and a couple clarifications: 

- Burst profile: correct on the peaks — we see short 30–90s spikes during new release campaigns. We can't shift the business requirement there.
- 120 ms p95: aspirational. For MVP we can accept up to 200 ms p95 if we get consistent behavior and clear rollbacks. Goal for GA is 120 ms p95.
- Heartbeat: 20s was a typo on our side — we meant 20s as an upper bound for perceived staleness, but we're happy to stick with a 15–30s SSE heartbeat. We do NOT want more aggressive client heartbeats (<5s) to avoid extra churn.
- Chunk cadence: 150–300 ms between chunks is what our UX lead prefers. We can tolerate 300–400 ms if overall p95 initial emission is improved.

Also: two technical Qs for Redwood team (please Cc any engineers):
1) How do you behave when a client disconnects mid-stream — do you hold the compute for N seconds waiting for reconnect (session stickiness), or do you let the model run to completion and drop the output?
2) When returned chunks are small, do you recommend priming tokens to avoid large relative overhead (you mentioned prefix caching on the call)?

Hi Samira — quick technical replies to your two Qs: 

1) Client disconnect mid-stream: by default our hosted runtime will continue the model invocation for a short grace window (configurable, default 10s). If the client reconnects and presents the same request/session id within the grace window we can resume streaming the remainder from the KV cache checkpoint. If not, we stop streaming and mark the invocation as aborted. For Dedicated/Private deployments we can extend the grace window or enable sticky sessions for longer but that consumes capacity and can increase cost.

2) Small chunk overhead / priming: small chunks can suffer higher per-chunk overhead. Two options we recommend:
   - Prefix caching (for repeated prompts): cache the KV for the common prompt prefix so initial emission only needs to compute continuation; this typically reduces initial emission by 30–60% for repeated flows.
   - Chunk batching (runtime option): emit slightly larger chunks (e.g., 6–8 tokens) at the client cadence to amortize per-chunk overhead while still allowing progressive UI updates.

On the 120 ms p95 initial emission goal — for the prompt sizes you described and at 50 concurrent steady users we are optimistic we can hit ~100–130 ms p95 with prefix caching and a small dedicated pool for your pilot. Microbursts to 350 req/s will require burst capacity reservations or a short-lived autoscale ramp; we should plan a pilot with a 1.5x burst headroom commitment to avoid degradation.

I'll draft a short tech appendix with recommended heartbeat settings, grace window, and chunk size tradeoffs (will attach).

—Rishi
